questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish Service Cloud from the bare Salesforce Platform?
options: They are identical products with different names

Service Cloud ships with a data model and processes oriented around support (Cases, Entitlements, Knowledge, omni-channel); the Platform is the unopinionated base with no vertical-specific data model baked in
The Platform always includes every Service Cloud feature by default
Service Cloud is only available to external users, never internal employees
questions.explain: Service Cloud bakes in a support-oriented data model and process set, while the core Platform provides objects, Flow, Apex, and Lightning without any vertical-specific model already built in.

questions.q: What is Experience Cloud specifically built for, according to this lesson?
options: Internal sales pipeline tracking
Exposing a branded, permission-scoped site to external users such as customers or partners, rather than internal employees
Running batch Apex jobs on a schedule
Hosting Salesforce's own internal admin tools
questions.explain: Experience Cloud is specifically the product for building a branded, permission-scoped external-facing site, distinct from the internal-employee focus of Sales or Service Cloud.

questions.q: In the build/configure/buy spectrum this lesson describes, why is 'configure a standard feature' generally preferred when the fit is genuinely good?
options: Because custom-built features are always technically superior
Because it's cheapest to build and cheapest to maintain, since Salesforce owns upgrading and supporting the standard feature
Because standard features cannot be customized at all
Because configuring a standard feature requires no requirements analysis
questions.explain: A standard feature that's configured rather than rebuilt from scratch shifts ongoing upgrade and support burden onto Salesforce itself, making it the cheapest option to build and maintain when the fit is genuinely good.

questions.q: What mistake does this lesson specifically warn against regarding the build/configure/buy spectrum?
options: Always choosing to buy from AppExchange regardless of fit
Skipping straight to 'build fully custom' because it feels like more control, without first honestly checking whether a standard object or feature already covers most of the requirement
Ever using a standard object for any requirement
Using Experience Cloud for internal-only applications
questions.explain: The lesson's core warning is against defaulting to full custom build out of a feeling of control, rather than first honestly assessing whether a standard object or feature already does most of the job.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call licensing an 'architectural constraint' rather than just a procurement detail?
options: Because a technically sound design can still fail in practice if it assumes license capabilities the actual user base doesn't hold, such as assuming full CRM functionality for users who only have a more limited license type
Because licensing has no bearing on what a design can actually do
Because only Technical Architects, never Application Architects, need to consider licensing
Because licensing questions should always be deferred until after user acceptance testing
questions.explain: A feature that assumes every user has full CRM capability, when a portion of the actual user base holds a more limited license type, is architecturally broken for its intended audience -- which is why checking license types belongs in requirements and design, not as a late surprise.
